headline: US midterm voting day lands on top of a stubborn tech sell-off, a fresh US strike on Iran, and another central bank rate rise in Australia. Meanwhile private credit, AI financing and a mega-merger in optical networking keep the dealmakers busy.

paragraphs.text: Distress and restructuring led the biotech news. Karyopharm, the multiple myeloma drugmaker, has filed for Chapter 11 after recently striking a forbearance deal to delay debt payments. Fierce Biotech and BioPharma Dive both report that Ayrmid, the Irish company that previously tried to buy bluebird, will be the lead bidder in a court-supervised auction, with a hematology merger as the goal. Endpoints says few options were left. The structure, a stalking-horse bid inside a bankruptcy sale, is the standard route for a commercial-stage biotech whose debt load outran its sales. For credit investors it is another reminder of how little room small-cap biotech has once covenants bite.

paragraphs.text: On the regulatory side, the FDA gave uniQure's Huntington's disease gene therapy priority review, with a decision date of May 1 and an advisory committee scheduled. Endpoints calls the program high-profile, and Fierce calls it a defining milestone. Inovio's Voceryq, described as the first plasmid DNA-based immunotherapy, won approval for a rare HPV-driven airway disease after an earlier scare over the accelerated pathway. Inovio led Nasdaq gainers on Monday. The FDA also approved a generic HIV prevention shot, a step toward wider access in lower-income countries, per STAT. Setbacks included a partial clinical hold on Bright Minds' seizure drug BMB-101 over toxicity in mouse studies, and a partial hold Gilead disclosed on two KITE-753 CAR-T trials in DLBCL. Teva stopped one trial for futility. FDA inspection reports also flagged sterilization problems at a Hansoh facility and data falsification concerns at a Samsung Biologics site, which is relevant to contract manufacturing diligence.

paragraphs.text: Biosimilars and licensing continued to draw attention. Fresenius signed what Endpoints calls one of the largest biosimilar deals to date with WuXi Biologics, covering up to 37 assets and as many as 66 molecules aimed at originator products worth more than 370 billion euros, per Fierce Pharma. BioPharma Dive separately argues that Keytruda biosimilars face an uphill climb despite the approaching patent cliff for Merck's flagship drug. AbbVie disclosed a deal with Beijing-based Brise Pharma for two preclinical migraine programs, though Brise says the agreement actually dates from 2024. Biossil Labs, backed by OpenAI, bought Theriva's deprioritised antibiotic-degrading enzyme portfolio for up to $91 million. Setara launched with $90 million to pursue rare disease genetics. In trial data, InventisBio's TYK2 inhibitor hit its phase 3 psoriasis endpoint. Tiziana's intranasal MS drug met its phase 2a endpoints, but the higher dose missed a neuroinflammation goal. Investors are also watching a Kymera eczema readout meant to challenge Dupixent, though STAT gave no date in the blurb.

paragraphs.text: Earnings and the policy backdrop were uneven. BioPharma Dive's roundup says AstraZeneca is launching a restructuring programme to redeploy resources, Alnylam sold off on worries about a top drug, and Regeneron was rewarded for a record quarter. Community Health Systems cut its 2026 earnings forecast and slid into the red in the third quarter. It blamed more uninsured patients, previously on ACA plans, seeking care, and deferred elective surgeries. That fits KFF's finding that Medicare Part D premiums will jump about 50% on average next year, and the Times report that ACA premiums will rise an average 13% for 2027 on top of an earlier steep increase. The FTC sent warning letters to 25 insurance marketers as open enrollment began. UnitedHealthcare will drop prior authorization on more than 2,000 pediatric codes from Dec. 1. Brigham and Women's nurses set Nov. 12 for an open-ended strike. Fierce Healthcare reports advisers expect hospitals to get little policy relief whatever the midterm outcome. Elsewhere, a Washington state resident died of bird flu after exposure to infected cattle, the first such US death in a year per STAT, and the NYT says the administration plans to roll back pregnancy-related job protections.

paragraphs.text: US equities start Tuesday on the back foot. The S&P 500 and Nasdaq opened November with losses as tech was sold on Monday, CNBC says, and MarketWatch reports the Nasdaq-100 has fallen into its third correction this year as AI worries mount. The Times says investors are bracing for more volatility, and the FT warns that the risk of higher volatility is rising after the recent resilience of equities. A leveraged Nasdaq-100 ETF burned traders who bought the dip last month, per MarketWatch. Beneath the index, the picture is different. CNBC says the average stock is having its best relative performance in decades, and the S&P 500's two straight losing months came from only a handful of names. MarketWatch adds that the most-hated stocks are beating the favourites, and that the index's forward P/E is now below its five- and ten-year averages after five months of going nowhere.

paragraphs.text: Company results fed the AI debate. Apple's shares fell even though iPhone demand is strong. The FT says it warned that unprecedented memory chip costs will hit margins, and the holiday sales forecast is robust but the services outlook disappointed. The Journal says new CEO John Ternus cautioned that margins may weaken in coming quarters. Palantir beat expectations and, in a notable shift, US commercial revenue overtook government revenue, per the Journal and MarketWatch. The stock still fell because US commercial contract growth decelerated, MarketWatch reports. The FT also says Nvidia has told cloud clients that most of their customers must be non-Chinese. Elliott, the $80 billion hedge fund, posted flat third-quarter returns and under 2% this year through September, and warned of what it called the fear of getting obliterated.

paragraphs.text: Midterm voting is the day's main event. The FT frames it as a referendum on the president, and its poll finds a big majority of voters disapprove of his handling of inflation. FT data show average petrol prices in his second term have passed Biden-era levels. CNBC notes midterms have historically preceded a strong year for the S&P 500. The FT says a Democratic sweep would bring big changes on energy and trade. The Journal says Wall Street is also watching races in states where there may be pushback on AI infrastructure. State Street expects different responses across Asian currencies, while the WSJ Dollar Index slipped to 97.00, its fourth straight decline.

paragraphs.text: The geopolitical picture is mixed for oil. The US struck Iran's Qeshm Island on the eve of the vote, which Washington called a defensive step against possible Iranian surface-to-air missile use, and the FT says oil was steady. Earlier, oil fell on hopes of US-Iran talks, and Bloomberg says Middle East flows now point to supply outrunning demand for the first time since July. Saudi Aramco's third-quarter profit rose 9% as the Iran war lifted prices, with its selling price about 35% higher than a year earlier.

paragraphs.text: Central banks keep tightening. The RBA raised its cash rate 25 basis points to 4.85%, the highest since 2008 and its fifth increase this year, after materially lifting its inflation forecasts. The Journal says the Bank of England is expected to hike Thursday, after the Fed, ECB and BoJ each raised at least once since the US-Iran war began. South Korea's inflation eased to 2.8% but stays above target, which supports further tightening. The PBOC raised the FX reserve requirement to 6% to steady the yuan, and BNP says China's forward earnings outlook keeps softening. US manufacturing PMI rose to 55.5, while Canada's slipped to 49.6. India's finance minister said she will consider equity gains tax changes amid a prolonged market slump.

paragraphs.text: Leveraged finance is showing strain. PitchBook's October wrap says loan prices fell as the sell-off broadened beyond software, and Pensions & Investments reports rising US leveraged loan distress that could foreshadow higher defaults. The blurbs give no figures, so the size of the move is unclear. Still, the direction matches the Alstom story in Europe: the FT says the French train maker's shares fell 26% after a second profit warning under its new chief, and it plans to cut €2 billion of debt. Elsewhere, Kalkine says credit jitters are growing around Australian lender Qualitas.

paragraphs.text: AI financing is the other worry. The Times's DealBook says investors are increasingly concerned about the debt-fuelled spending behind the AI build-out. FT Alphaville says data centre construction delays are getting awkward for investors, and CNBC notes CoreWeave has sold off amid debt concerns, though one contrarian sees upside. In private credit, Bloomberg says CPPIB is warning of the next big headache for investors, but the blurb gives no detail. Related-party lending is drawing scrutiny: the FT reports Todd Boehly's insurer Security Benefit has amassed more than $3 billion of loans tied to his Beverly Hills real estate project, as regulators watch insurers that lend to owner-affiliated companies.

paragraphs.text: Capital keeps flowing into the asset class. Man Group's private credit push has won backing from Japanese insurers, per Kalkine and Simply Wall St. Neo raised ₹6,200 crore for a second credit fund aiming for 35-40 investments, and Alternatives Watch says Abu Dhabi sovereign funds are backing new credit and infrastructure platforms. In Europe, the FT describes a dispute between banks and insurers over the Danish compromise, which makes it easier for eurozone banks to own insurers, and insurers say it gives banks an unfair edge. US bank supervision produced two small items: the FDIC's inspector general says mortgage expansion killed Tioga-Franklin, and the FDIC eased its directive on Old Glory Bank to adequately capitalized. Separately, Bangladesh's private sector credit growth stays under 5%.

paragraphs.text: The largest transaction is in technology. Marvell and Lumentum announced an all-stock combination valued at $115 billion, a bet on optical networking in AI data centres, per the Times. Shares of both companies fell Monday, and MarketWatch quotes shareholders on both sides panning the terms, one calling it a trash offer. Goldman's David Solomon told Bloomberg he sees very robust demand for AI deals and expects a technology supercycle to dominate capital markets and financing. That bullish view clashes with the day's tech sell-off.

paragraphs.text: Anthropic's IPO is looming. WSJ coverage cited by TradingView says investors are urging caution on pricing, with a target valuation of $1.5 trillion to $1.6 trillion, though the headline does not make clear who set that target. Bloomberg says revenue is nearing $17 billion, and The Hindu says revenue surged 1,100%, with no period given in either list entry. In energy, the Journal reports Carl Icahn's CVR Energy is near a deal worth over $4 billion for Marathon Petroleum refineries, as global conflicts boost US refiners' sales. Alternatives Watch also reports Stonepeak's Castrol deal and Brookfield's $5.2 billion REIT take-private among a day of closings.
